turns.text: how do SGLT2 inhibitors lower blood sugar

paragraphs.text: They work at the kidney, not the pancreas. Glucose gets filtered at the glomerulus, and normally almost all of it is reabsorbed by the sodium-glucose transporter. turns.text: What is C-peptide and why would you measure it?

paragraphs.text: C-peptide is the leftover piece from making insulin. Beta cells build proinsulin, then cut it into insulin (the A and B chains) plus C-peptide, the bit that held the chains together. The two come out in equal amounts.

paragraphs.text: Why measure it: an insulin level can't tell injected insulin from the patient's own, but injected insulin carries no C-peptide. turns.text: What do Sertoli cells do?

paragraphs.text: Dr. Herr calls Sertoli cells "the refrigerator": they feed and support the developing sperm. Each one is tall and columnar, reaching from the basement membrane to the lumen. turns.text: When would you pick lingualized occlusion for a denture?

paragraphs.text: Short version from Dr. Givan's L8 notes: lingualized is the scheme you'd reach for with almost anyone. It's hugely popular because the teeth are much easier to arrange, it can be set balanced or non-balanced, and it works with any ridge morphology, so with almost any patient, young to old. It's widely used in the school's clinic.

cites.label: L8 notes
cites.quote: it works with any ridge morphology, so with almost any patient, young to old

paragraphs.text: The real decision is how to set it, based on what the patient brings. Set it non-balanced for a lot of ridge resorption, flabby tissues, poor oral awareness or dexterity, or difficult jaw relations. Set it balanced for healthy patients with good ridges, firm mucosa, and good awareness and muscular dexterity. The trade-off is that with fewer teeth touching, wear shows sooner and the patient may lose VDO.

turns.text: what's abfraction

paragraphs.text: Abfraction is loss of tooth structure from flexural loading: a notch near the CEJ, usually on the facial. Dr. Lawson (L9) explains it like this: a load the tooth shouldn't have lands on an inclined plane and pushes the crown to one side. The tooth flexes about the fulcrum where it's anchored in bone. One side is compressed, the other is pulled apart, and teeth are weaker in tension, so the lesion forms on the tensile side, just above the fulcrum. His analogy: pushing on a stop sign.

cites.label: L7 notes
cites.quote: Loss of tooth structure from flexural biomechanical loading

cites.label: L9 notes
cites.quote: abfraction lesions can form, just above the fulcrum

paragraphs.text: Clues: exostoses and tori, opposing wear facets, generalized wear. Fix: a night guard, sacrificial plastic, not a TMD treatment. And Dr. Givan's caution: it's supported in vitro but clinically neither validated nor rejected, so he doesn't count it as a primary mechanism of wear.

cites.label: L9 notes
cites.quote: exostoses and tori sometimes accompany NCCLs

cites.label: L9 notes
cites.quote: clinical documentation has neither validated nor rejected it

paragraphs.text: As a molar, I take inclined-plane loads very personally.

turns.text: What's the Bennett movement?

paragraphs.text: Bennett movement is mandibular lateral translation: the sideways shift of the whole mandible toward the working side. It goes by several names, side shift among them. It can be immediate (a jump, measured in millimeters) or progressive (measured as an angle, the Bennett angle). It comes with joint laxity, and Dr. Givan said its clinical importance is still debated; know the definition, not the debate.

cites.label: L1 notes
cites.quote: the mediolateral shift of the mandible toward the working side

cites.label: L1 Exam Hints
cites.quote: Bennett movement / side shift: know the definition, not the debate.

paragraphs.text: Why it matters: more Bennett movement (or a bigger immediate side shift) means shorter posterior cusps, and it widens the angle between a cusp's working and non-working paths. On a semi-adjustable articulator, the Bennett angle is the setting Dr. Givan would leave off first, since average values are close enough.

cites.label: L1 notes
cites.quote: Greater, more superior, or greater immediate side shift · Shorter

cites.label: L1 notes
cites.quote: a greater Bennett movement all increase the angle

cites.label: L6 Exam Hints
cites.quote: The Bennett angle is the less commonly adjusted setting; SCI matters more.

paragraphs.text: Norman G. Bennett described it in 1908. A tooth with an eponym, now there's a dream.

turns.text: What's the freeway space and why does it matter?

paragraphs.text: Freeway space, also called interocclusal rest space, is the gap between the teeth when the jaw is at rest. It's vertical dimension at rest (VDR) minus vertical dimension of occlusion (VDO), usually 2-6 mm. Neither 2 nor 6 is "better." VDO is the face height with the teeth together, and it supports facial height.

cites.label: L1 notes
cites.quote: Freeway space (interocclusal rest space) = VDR minus VDO, usually 2-6 mm

paragraphs.text: The notes don't spell out why freeway space itself matters clinically. What they do cover nearby: losing VDO through posterior overclosure causes interferences and unhealthy loading, and the closest speaking space on "s" helps set a functional vertical dimension.

cites.label: L1 notes
cites.quote: loss of occluding vertical dimension as posterior teeth are lost or drift, causing interferences and unhealthy loading

cites.label: L3 notes
cites.quote: the closest speaking space helps set a functional vertical dimension

paragraphs.text: Two to six millimeters of breathing room. I keep mine generous, naturally.

turns.text: Why is it the mesial fossae of the maxillary premolars and not the distal?

paragraphs.text: Think about where the lower arch sits. In the help sheet's fence post, in Class I each mandibular post sits a half step mesial (in front of) its maxillary partner. With the lower teeth a half step forward, the mandibular premolar's buccal cusp lands toward the front of the upper premolar, in its mesial fossa. Going the other way, the upper premolar's lingual cusp lands toward the back of the lower premolar, in its distal fossa. So in Class I, the buccal cusp of #29 sits in the mesial fossa of #4, and the lingual cusp of #5 sits in the distal fossa of #28.

paragraphs.text: Your pick, B, is the Class II rule. Class II steps the mandible back one post, so everything flips: maxillary distal fossae, mandibular mesial fossae (#29 buccal cusp into the distal fossa of #4). Class III brings the mandible forward a whole tooth, which keeps the Class I pattern: #29's buccal cusp lands in the mesial fossa of #5.

turns.text: How do you stage periodontitis?

paragraphs.text: Staging measures how severe the disease is and how complex it will be to manage. Interdental CAL is the gold standard, and radiographic bone loss is the backup. Stage 1 is 1 to 2 mm of CAL and Stage 2 is 3 to 4 mm, both with bone loss in the coronal third. Stages 3 and 4 both have CAL of 5 mm or more, with bone loss into the middle third or beyond. What separates them is tooth loss to periodontitis (4 or fewer teeth for Stage 3, 5 or more for Stage 4) and whether the case needs complex rehabilitation.

cites.label: S1 review table

paragraphs.text: Three findings send a case straight to Stage 3 or 4: vertical bone loss of 3 mm or more, a Class II or III furcation, or any tooth lost to periodontitis. Each patient gets one stage, taken from the single worst site in the mouth. Dr. Abou-Arraj's warning, said twice in lecture: never stage from probing depth alone. Confirm attachment loss and bone loss first. A mouthful of 4s and 5s could be plain gingivitis. Even I get a 4 now and then, and I'm a model tooth.

turns.text: What's the difference between grade A, B and C?

paragraphs.text: Grading is about how fast the disease is moving. Start at Grade B (moderate) and only shift with evidence. Without serial records, divide percent bone loss on the worst tooth by age: under 0.25 suggests A (slow), 0.25 to 1.0 suggests B, over 1.0 suggests C (rapid).

cites.label: S1 review table
cites.quote: % bone loss ÷ age < 0.25 at the worst tooth

paragraphs.text: Direct evidence beats the ratio: over 5 years, no loss is A, under 2 mm is B, 2 mm or more is C. Then the modifiers, which only push up: heavy smoking (more than 10 a day) or HbA1c of 7% or higher sends a case straight to C. Nobody gets downgraded for not smoking.

turns.text: What are cervical enamel projections and why do they matter for furcations?

paragraphs.text: A cervical enamel projection (CEP) is a narrow, wedge-shaped strip of enamel that runs from the CEJ toward the furcation, like a widow's peak. It forms when amelogenesis fails to stop before root formation. Dr. Litz called it a definite test question and something to know for life.

cites.label: S5 notes
cites.quote: It forms when amelogenesis fails to halt before root formation

paragraphs.text: Why it matters: junctional epithelium and connective tissue can't attach to enamel, so the gingiva just lies over it. The CEP works like a funnel that leads plaque straight into the furcation. CEPs show up on about 30% of mandibular molars and 15% of maxillary ones, more on second molars and on the buccal.

cites.label: S5 notes
cites.quote: the CEP acts like a funnel leading plaque straight into the furcation

paragraphs.text: Grades: 1 dips toward the furcation, 2 approaches it, 3 enters it. With no bone or attachment loss, watch it. With loss, remove it with a bur, and warn about thermal sensitivity if it's thick. A lone furcation in an otherwise stable mouth? Look for a CEP. Enamel where it doesn't belong: even I find that tacky.

turns.text: How are furcations classified?

paragraphs.text: The main system is Glickman, the one Dr. Litz uses and the school uses too, read with a Nabers probe. Grade I is incipient: you feel the entrance, but the bone between the roots is intact. Grade II: that bone is lost, but not through to the other side, so the probe catches. Grade III is through-and-through, buccal to lingual. Grade IV is through-and-through with recession, so you can see through it. Dr. Kaur adds that Class II is the most regenerable.

turns.text: What is guided tissue regeneration?

paragraphs.text: Guided tissue regeneration (GTR) puts a barrier membrane over the defect, under the flap. The membrane keeps the fast-growing gingival epithelium and connective tissue away from the root, so cells from the PDL and bone can repopulate it instead. In the deck's cases, the regenerated bone was still there on radiographs at 20 and 25 years.

cites.label: S6 notes
cites.quote: A barrier membrane goes over the defect, under the flap.

paragraphs.text: Put a bone graft under the membrane and you have combination therapy: the graft holds the space so the membrane can't collapse into the defect. GTR works best in deep, narrow defects with more walls (deeper than 3 mm, angle of 25 degrees or less). With high esthetic risk, the decision tree says to avoid the membrane.

cites.quote: In combination therapy a bone graft goes under the membrane and holds the space

turns.text: connective tissue graft vs free gingival graft?

paragraphs.text: Both come from the palate, but they carry different layers. A free gingival graft (FGG) is the epithelium plus the lamina propria in one piece. A connective tissue graft (CTG) is just the connective tissue, with the epithelium removed.

cites.quote: the epithelium together with the lamina propria (the connective tissue) under it in one piece

turns.text: what's the deal with bisphosphonates in perio

paragraphs.text: Dr. Litz covered them under host modulation. On paper they look like the magic bullet: bone-seeking drugs that inhibit osteoclasts, maybe with an anticollagenase effect too. turns.text: what's the difference between gingivitis and periodontitis on a reduced periodontium?

paragraphs.text: A reduced periodontium is just one that has already lost some support, and that can come from prior periodontitis, crown lengthening or simple recession. It can be healthy or inflamed. Gingivitis on it means inflammation (bleeding, maybe 4 to 5 mm pockets from swelling) but no new attachment or bone loss. It stays in the gingiva and is reversible with plaque control.
